## I. Introduction

**Q.** Please state your name and business address.

**A.** My name is Juan-Pablo Velez, and my business address is 461 W 126th St #5W, New York, NY 10027.

**Q.** Are you the same Juan-Pablo Velez who filed direct testimony in this proceeding?

**A.** Yes. I filed direct testimony on behalf of the Chesapeake Climate Action Network on September 22, 2026.[^velez-direct]

[^velez-direct]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Chesapeake Climate Action Network](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct") (Sep. 22, 2026) [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

**Q.** What is the purpose of your surrebuttal testimony?

**A.** To respond to portions of the rebuttal testimony of BGE witness Jennifer A. Karas concerning my proposed heat pump rate, Schedule R-HP.

**Q.** Please summarize your surrebuttal testimony.

**A.** Ms. Karas does not dispute that BGE's heat pump customers are overcharged. Instead, she identifies three barriers to BGE adopting Schedule R-HP. I respond to each one, and I show that my overcharge finding holds up under different data, so the Commission should act on it now. In brief:

1. **Barrier 1: BGE says it lacks the data.** It has the data it says it lacks, and it did not provide it when CCAN asked.
2. **Barrier 2: BGE says it cannot develop the schedule without eligibility rules.** Eligibility rules are developed as part of creating a schedule, not before it, and I have already proposed them.
3. **Barrier 3: BGE says participants would need smart meters.** BGE has already installed them across nearly all of its residential class.

I also show that my overcharge finding does not depend on the BGE data Ms. Karas objects to: an independent analysis using ResStock finds a similar overcharge. Since none of the three barriers is real, and two independent sources show a similar overcharge, there is no reason for the Commission to delay.

**Q.** Does your silence on any other part of Ms. Karas's rebuttal testimony mean that you agree with it?

**A.** No.

## II. BGE Does Not Dispute That Heat Pump Customers Are Overcharged

**Q.** Please restate the central finding of your direct testimony.

**A.** When a BGE customer replaces a fossil fuel heating system with a heat pump, their distribution and transmission charges rise by an average of `{python} dollar(d.all_fossil_annual_delivery_charges_delta)` per year, while the new distribution and transmission costs they cause rise by only `{python} dollar(mc_delta(d))`. Including EmPOWER Maryland charges, heat pump customers are overcharged by an average of `{python} dollar(d.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge)` per year.[^finding] To end this cross-subsidy, I recommended Schedule R-HP, with distribution, transmission, and EmPOWER rates that are `{python} pct(-d.rhp_pct_change_dist)`, `{python} pct(-d.rhp_pct_change_tx)`, and `{python} pct(-d.rhp_pct_change_empower)` lower than Schedule R's.[^recs]

[^finding]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 5:17, 14:10–13 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

[^recs]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 6:21–7:12 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

**Q.** Does Ms. Karas dispute this finding?

**A.** No. Ms. Karas does not offer her own estimate of the costs heat pump customers cause or of the charges they pay. Nor does she dispute that charging one group of residential customers far more than the costs they cause is an intra-class inequity; elsewhere in her rebuttal, she invokes that very principle to support BGE's proposed customer charge.[^karas-intraclass] Her only objection to the analysis itself concerns its data, which I address next.

[^karas-intraclass]: [Rebuttal Testimony of Jennifer A. Karas on behalf of Baltimore Gas and Electric Company](https://pub.switch.box/karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026) ("Karas Rebuttal"), at 13:14–15 (Oct. 16, 2026) (when fixed costs "are not recovered through fixed charges, intra-class inequities are created or allowed to persist") [@karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026].

## III. The Overcharge Does Not Depend on BGE's Heating Subclass

**Q.** Ms. Karas states that your analysis "relies on BGE data identifying 'heating' and 'non-heating' indications ... and not on actual verified BGE heat-pump customers."[^karas-data] Is that accurate?

[^karas-data]: [Karas Rebuttal](https://pub.switch.box/karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026) at 22:3–5 [@karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026].

**A.** It is true that none of my analysis uses load data from verified BGE heat pump customers, but not for lack of asking. CCAN asked BGE for exactly that data: the number of its residential customers who heat with a heat pump, their electricity consumption, and their hourly load. BGE answered that it "does not track customers by known heat source and, therefore, is not able to provide hourly data for customers with a heat pump as their primary heating source."[^asked-hp]

[^asked-hp]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026), Ex. JPV-5, [BGE Response to CCAN DR 1-3](https://pub.switch.box/bge_Docket9888Response_2026); _id._, Ex. JPV-6, [BGE Response to CCAN DR 1-8](https://pub.switch.box/bge_Docket9888Response_2026) [@bge_Docket9888Response_2026].

So I relied on the next best data, and not only BGE's. My direct testimony looked at heat pump adoption in two ways, using two different sources of data.

First, to measure the overcharge, I looked at the _average_ fossil-fuel-heated home in BGE's territory, before and after it switches to a heat pump (Section III, Figures 1–11). For this, I used BGE's monthly and hourly metered consumption data, which BGE reports separately for its non-heating and electric-heating residential customers. For "before," I averaged the consumption of BGE's non-heating residential customers on Schedules R and RL, who heat with natural gas, oil, propane, or another non-electric fuel; for "after," I averaged the consumption of its electric-heating residential customers, on Schedules RH and RLH.[^bge-data] This comparison produced the `{python} dollar(d.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge)` annual overcharge, the `{python} dollar(d.all_fossil_annual_delivery_charges_delta)` in added charges against `{python} dollar(mc_delta(d))` in added costs, and the proposed Schedule R-HP rate reductions. It is the only part of my analysis that relies on BGE's subclass data. That was the most granular data BGE was willing to provide, and I disclosed that its electric-heating subclass mixes heat pump homes with electric resistance homes.[^disclosed]

[^bge-data]: Charges and costs came from different BGE data. For charges, BGE's monthly data gives each subclass's total number of customers and total kWh sales in each month. Dividing total kWh by total customers gives the average monthly consumption of a non-heating customer and of an electric-heating customer; applying BGE's filed Schedule R rates to each gives their average monthly bills, and the difference between the two is the increase in charges. For costs, I needed to know _when_ that consumption occurs, because new T&D costs are driven by consumption during peak hours. I therefore used BGE's hourly data for each subclass to spread the average customer's consumption across the hours of the year, and multiplied each hour's consumption by that hour's marginal T&D cost. [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 64:14–17, 65:12–17, 68:8–18 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026]; _id._, Ex. JPV-2, [BGE Response to CCAN DR 1-4, Attach. 1](https://pub.switch.box/bge_Docket9888CCANDR0104_2026) (monthly kWh sales and customer counts by subclass, April 2025–March 2026) [@bge_Docket9888CCANDR0104_2026]; _id._, Ex. JPV-3, [BGE Response to CCAN DR 1-11, Attach. 1](https://pub.switch.box/bge_Docket9888CCANDR0111_2026) (hourly kWh by subclass, 2024) [@bge_Docket9888CCANDR0111_2026].

Second, to show how bills would change for _all_ of BGE's homes, not just the average one, I used ResStock, a building simulation model from the National Laboratory of the Rockies ("NLR"), which models 4,897 individual BGE-territory homes, each before and after a heat pump retrofit (Sections IV and VI, Figures 12–19). This is where my finding that Schedule R-HP would make it cheaper to heat with heat pumps than with fossil fuels for `{python} pct(b.pct_all_fossil_hp_bill_decrease_rhp)` of fossil-fuel-heated BGE homes comes from. These results do not use BGE's subclass at all, and they model heat pumps specifically, not electric heating in general.[^resstock-pop]

[^disclosed]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 69:4–11 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

[^resstock-pop]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 71:8–72:2 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

**Q.** Does Ms. Karas claim that relying on BGE's subclass data changes your finding?

**A.** No. She does not say that it changes the overcharge, in which direction it would bias it, or by how much; she lists it only among the barriers to implementing the rate.[^karas-barrier]

[^karas-barrier]: [Karas Rebuttal](https://pub.switch.box/karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026) at 21:19–22:5 [@karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026].

**Q.** Did you nonetheless test whether mixing in electric resistance homes affects your finding?

**A.** Yes. I redid the average-home comparison with ResStock in place of BGE's subclass data: instead of comparing two different groups of BGE customers, I took the average of the same fossil-fuel-heated BGE homes in ResStock, once with their existing natural gas, oil, or propane heating and once after a cold-climate heat pump retrofit. That comparison contains no electric resistance homes, and it measures the same homes before and after. The results are close to those in my direct testimony (Table 1).[^rerun]

[^rerun]: Computed from NLR's ResStock 2024.2 building stock model for Maryland, restricted to BGE-territory buildings heated with natural gas, heating oil, or propane, comparing each building's baseline with its heat pump retrofit, with the corrections described in [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 70:13–71:7; bills computed with the CAIRO model using BGE's filed Schedule R rates. NREL, _End-Use Load Profiles for the U.S. Building Stock_ (2024), https://doi.org/10.25984/1876417.

_Table 1: Annual change for the average fossil-fuel-heated BGE home that switches to a heat pump, measured with BGE's customer data and with ResStock._

| | BGE customer data (direct testimony) | ResStock (same homes, before and after) |
| --- | :---: | :---: |
| Added electricity use | `{python} comma(d.all_fossil_annual_kwh_delta)` kWh | `{python} comma(s.all_fossil_annual_kwh_delta)` kWh |
| Added distribution and transmission charges | `{python} dollar(d.all_fossil_annual_delivery_charges_delta)` | `{python} dollar(s.all_fossil_annual_delivery_charges_delta)` |
| Added EmPOWER Maryland charges | `{python} dollar(d.all_fossil_annual_empower_maryland_delta)` | `{python} dollar(s.all_fossil_annual_empower_maryland_delta)` |
| Added distribution and transmission costs | `{python} dollar(mc_delta(d))` | `{python} dollar(mc_delta(s))` |
| **Overcharge** | **`{python} dollar(d.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge)`** | **`{python} dollar(s.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge)`** |
| Schedule R-HP distribution rate reduction | `{python} pct(-d.rhp_pct_change_dist)` | `{python} pct(-s.rhp_pct_change_dist)` |
| Schedule R-HP transmission rate reduction | `{python} pct(-d.rhp_pct_change_tx)` | `{python} pct(-s.rhp_pct_change_tx)` |
| Schedule R-HP EmPOWER rate reduction | `{python} pct(-d.rhp_pct_change_empower)` | `{python} pct(-s.rhp_pct_change_empower)` |

**Q.** What do you conclude?

**A.** That the overcharge is not an artifact of BGE's subclass data. The two analyses are built in very different ways: one compares two different groups of real BGE customers, using BGE's own metered data; the other simulates a sample of BGE-territory homes whose size, insulation, heating systems, and other characteristics are drawn from federal survey data on the local building stock, and models the same homes before and after a heat pump retrofit, with no electric resistance homes.[^survey] Yet they arrive at nearly the same result. Both find that a heat pump adds about the same amount of electricity use and about the same distribution and transmission charges, and that the new costs it causes are a small fraction of those added charges. Under either source, BGE would overcharge the average fossil-fuel-heated home that switches to a heat pump by roughly `{python} dollar(min(d.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge, s.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge))` to `{python} dollar(max(d.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge, s.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge))` a year (Table 1).

[^survey]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 70:5–8 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

The reason is also the same in both sources: most of the electricity a heat pump adds is used in winter, while BGE's distribution and transmission costs are driven mainly by summer peaks.[^summer]

[^summer]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 16:6–9 (80% of distribution peak hours and 82% of bulk transmission peak hours fall between May and September) [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

**Q.** What is ResStock, and what is its track record?

**A.** ResStock is developed by NLR, the U.S. Department of Energy's ("DOE") laboratory for energy efficiency research, and simulates every hour of a statistically representative sample of Maryland's building stock using DOE's EnergyPlus engine.[^resstock-what] NLR calibrated and validated it against U.S. Energy Information Administration ("EIA") utility sales data, utility load research data, and smart meter data from utilities across the country.[^calibrated] Massachusetts's Interagency Rates Working Group also relied on this dataset to develop the heat pump rates it proposed to the state's Department of Public Utilities.[^e3] ISO New England builds its heat pump adoption and winter peak forecasts using ResStock, and the DOE recommends it for utility load forecasting, distribution planning, and electrification planning.[^doe-isone]

ResStock also matches BGE's own data. ResStock's typical fossil-fuel-heated BGE home uses `{python} comma(s.all_fossil_annual_kwh_before)` kWh per year, within `{python} pct(1 - s.all_fossil_annual_kwh_before / d.all_fossil_annual_kwh_before)` of the `{python} comma(d.all_fossil_annual_kwh_before)` kWh used by BGE's average non-electric-heating residential customer.

[^resstock-what]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 70:1–12 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

[^calibrated]: RIPUC Docket No. 25-45-GE, _Application of The Narragansett Electric Company d/b/a Rhode Island Energy for Approval of a Change in Electric and Gas Base Distribution Rates_, [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket2545GEPreFiled_2026) ("Velez RI Direct"), at 75:4–6 (Apr. 16, 2026) [@velez_Docket2545GEPreFiled_2026].

[^doe-isone]: [_Id._](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket2545GEPreFiled_2026) at 75:6–8 [@velez_Docket2545GEPreFiled_2026].

[^e3]: Energy and Environmental Economics, [_Near-Term Rate Design to Align with the Commonwealth's Decarbonization Goals_](https://pub.switch.box/e3_NearTermRateDesign_2024), prepared for the Massachusetts Interagency Rates Working Group, at 80 (Dec. 2024) ("representative households were selected from NREL's public ResStock database version 2024.2") [@e3_NearTermRateDesign_2024]; D.P.U. 25-08, _Inquiry by the Department of Public Utilities on its own Motion into a Seasonal Heat Pump Rate_, [Petition of the Department of Energy Resources](https://pub.switch.box/doer_Docket2508Petition_2025), at 7 (Jan. 31, 2025) (attaching the E3 report as Exhibit A and the Working Group's recommendations as Exhibit B) [@doer_Docket2508Petition_2025].

## IV. Barrier 1: BGE Has the Data It Says It Lacks

**Q.** Ms. Karas states that BGE "does not have specific knowledge of customer heating sources and does not have sufficient data to support an electric heat-pump rate design."[^karas-nodata] Do you agree?

[^karas-nodata]: [Karas Rebuttal](https://pub.switch.box/karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026) at 22:1–3 [@karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026].

**A.** No. BGE does not record heating systems in its billing system, but it knows which of its customers have installed heat pumps. BGE administers the EmPOWER Maryland programs that pay heat pump incentives in its territory, and it reported 10,070 heat pump installations through those programs in 2025 alone, nearly double the number in 2024.[^empower-hps] Its midstream heat pump rebate applications require the address and BGE account number of the home where each heat pump is installed.[^account]

[^empower-hps]: Case No. 9705, _The 2024-2026 EmPOWER Maryland Program_, [Maryland Office of People's Counsel, Comments on EmPOWER Maryland 2025 Q3-Q4 Semi-Annual Reports](https://pub.switch.box/mdopc_Docket9705Comments_2026), at 41–42 (Apr. 15, 2026) ("BGE reported the largest level of HVAC participation in the state, with 10,070 heat pumps installed during 2025," "nearly doubling participation from 2024") [@mdopc_Docket9705Comments_2026].

[^account]: HVAC Distributors, [_Maryland Rebates_](https://pub.switch.box/hvacdistributors_MarylandRebates_nd) (last accessed Oct. 29, 2026) (BGE midstream program documentation required: "BGE customer installation address and associated account #") [@hvacdistributors_MarylandRebates_nd].

**Q.** Does BGE have usage data for those customers?

**A.** Yes. BGE reports that it has installed smart meters across its residential class, and 98% of its residential meters were smart meters at the end of 2025.[^eia-ami] BGE also already prepares study-quality load data from AMI interval readings.[^ami] Matching the account numbers on its EmPOWER heat pump rebate records to this usage data would give BGE the verified heat pump load data Ms. Karas says it lacks.

[^eia-ami]: [EIA, Form EIA-861 Advanced Meters, 2025 Data Year](https://pub.switch.box/eia_FormEIA861Detailed_2026), row "Baltimore Gas & Electric Co": 1,214,908 advanced metering infrastructure ("AMI") meters and 23,584 automated meter reading meters out of 1,238,492 residential meters (released Oct. 7, 2026) [@eia_FormEIA861Detailed_2026].

[^ami]: [Direct Testimony of Jennifer A. Karas on behalf of Baltimore Gas and Electric Company](https://pub.switch.box/karas_Docket9888Direct_2026) ("Karas Direct"), at 20:5–8 (July 2, 2026) [@karas_Docket9888Direct_2026]; [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026), Ex. JPV-3, [BGE Response to CCAN DR 1-11](https://pub.switch.box/bge_Docket9888Response_2026) (study-quality load data requires "extraction of AMI interval data") [@bge_Docket9888Response_2026].

**Q.** Did you ask BGE for this data?

**A.** Yes. CCAN asked BGE for aggregated hourly load data for its heat pump customers. BGE answered that it "does not track customers by known heat source" and that it "has not prepared the requested analysis."[^drs] BGE's response reflects analysis it has not done, not data it does not have.

[^drs]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026), Ex. JPV-6, [BGE Response to CCAN DR 1-8](https://pub.switch.box/bge_Docket9888Response_2026); _id._, Ex. JPV-8, [BGE Response to CCAN DR 1-7](https://pub.switch.box/bge_Docket9888Response_2026) [@bge_Docket9888Response_2026].

**Q.** Have other utilities adopted heat pump rates without data on verified heat pump customers?

**A.** Yes. None of Massachusetts's three electric utilities based its heat pump rate on metered data from verified heat pump customers. Unitil estimated heat pump consumption by converting its gas heating customers' usage to electricity at heat pump efficiencies, and Eversource did the same; Eversource conceded it had not analyzed the actual usage of its heat pump customers. National Grid stated that it lacked the data even to estimate how many heat pumps were on its system.[^ma] The Department of Public Utilities approved heat pump rates for all three.[^ma-orders] My analysis rests on stronger evidence: BGE's own metered data, corroborated by ResStock. And as demonstrated above, BGE does in fact have the ability to collect data on verified heat pump customers; it has simply declined to do so.

[^ma]: D.P.U. 23-80, _Fitchburg Gas and Electric Light Company d/b/a Unitil_, [Direct Testimony of John D. Taylor](https://pub.switch.box/taylor_Docket2380Direct_2023), Exh. Unitil-JDT-1, at 24:16–17 (Aug. 17, 2023) (gas heating customers' normal use "was converted to an equivalent kWh usage based on the efficiency of heat pumps") [@taylor_Docket2380Direct_2023]; D.P.U. 25-55, _Petition of NSTAR Electric Company d/b/a Eversource Energy for Approval of Residential Seasonal Heat Pump Rates_, [Direct Testimony of Richard D. HP-1](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024), at 4 (Dec. 30, 2024) (National Grid "does not have sufficient data to support an estimate of the total number of existing heat-pumps") [@meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024].

## V. The Commission Should Adopt Schedule R-HP Now

**Q.** Should the Commission wait for BGE to collect verified heat pump data before adopting Schedule R-HP?

**A.** I do not think this is necessary. Two independent sources, BGE's metered data and ResStock, find a similar overcharge and call for approximately the same rate reductions, and BGE offers no evidence to the contrary. Each year of delay is another year in which BGE's heat pump customers pay hundreds of dollars more than the costs they cause.

My direct testimony already recommends recalibrating Schedule R-HP's rates in BGE's next rate case.[^recalibrate] The Commission can direct BGE to perform that recalibration with its EmPOWER heat pump records and smart meter data, which would answer Ms. Karas's concern without prolonging the overcharge.

However, if the Commission deems it necessary to measure the overcharge using BGE's verified heat pump usage data before adopting Schedule R-HP, the data collection and analysis that would be required are not complicated, and they should take BGE no more than a couple of months. BGE already has what it needs: the account numbers on its EmPOWER heat pump rebates and the same smart meter extraction process it uses to prepare load data for its cost-of-service study.[^ami-process]

[^ami-process]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026), Ex. JPV-3, [BGE Response to CCAN DR 1-11](https://pub.switch.box/bge_Docket9888Response_2026) at 1 (describing the steps for preparing "study-quality load data," starting with "extraction of AMI interval data") [@bge_Docket9888Response_2026].

[^recalibrate]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 7:19–21 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

## VI. Barrier 2: Eligibility Rules Are Part of Creating the Schedule

**Q.** Ms. Karas states that BGE would need a Commission-approved process to determine eligibility, as it developed for Schedule EV.[^karas-ev] Is that an obstacle to adopting Schedule R-HP?

[^karas-ev]: [Karas Rebuttal](https://pub.switch.box/karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026) at 22:5–10 [@karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026].

**A.** No. Ms. Karas has the sequence backwards. She says BGE cannot offer Schedule R-HP because it lacks a Commission-approved process for verifying who qualifies. My direct testimony proposes the creation of a new rate schedule. Setting eligibility rules is part of the process of creating a new rate schedule, not a precondition for it. Her own example shows this: BGE's Schedule EV was approved together with its eligibility terms, as part of creating that rate.[^ev-order]

[^ev-order]: [Maryland PSC, _Electric Vehicle Pilot Program Report_](https://pub.switch.box/mdpsc_ElectricVehiclePilot_2015) at 1–2 (Jan. 30, 2015) (the Commission "issued Order No. 85776 approving EV pilot programs" for BGE and Pepco on Aug. 12, 2013; BGE's pilot "is available only to those residential customers who receive Standard Offer Service … do not participate in net metering, and do not purchase renewable energy from a third party") [@mdpsc_ElectricVehiclePilot_2015].

Indeed, my direct testimony proposed eligibility rules — which Ms. Karas did not acknowledge in her rebuttal — modeled on the Massachusetts heat pump rates: automatic enrollment of customers who received heat pump incentives through EmPOWER Maryland, plus an attestation and certification pathway for customers who installed heat pumps without one.[^enroll] As with Schedule EV,[^ev-order] the Commission could approve these rules, with or without modification, when it approves Schedule R-HP.

[^enroll]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 7:13–18, 45:9–14, 47:5–11 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

## VII. Barrier 3: Smart Meters Are Already Installed

**Q.** In addition to the lack of heating-source data and the need for an eligibility process, Ms. Karas identifies a third barrier to BGE implementing a heat pump rate schedule: "if electric supply time-of-use ('TOU') pricing were approved by the Commission, participants would be required to have smart meters capable of measuring hourly TOU data."[^karas-tou] Is this a real barrier?

[^karas-tou]: [Karas Rebuttal](https://pub.switch.box/karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026) at 22:14–16 [@karas_Docket9888Prepared_2026].

**A.** No. Smart meters are already nearly universal at BGE: 98% of its residential meters are smart meters,[^eia-ami] and Ms. Karas herself says BGE has installed them "across the residential class."[^smart] Moreover, Schedule R-HP only affects transmission, distribution, and EmPOWER,[^flat] and could easily be paired with a TOU supply rate. BGE already pairs supply TOU rates with distinct delivery rates: Schedule RD customers get TOU supply pricing together with time-varying delivery rates, which differ from Schedule R's.[^rd] A heat pump delivery rate could be paired with a TOU supply rate in the same way.

[^flat]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 5:4–5 [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

[^rd]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 50:4–11 (Schedule RD is available to all residential customers with a smart meter and, unlike the legacy TOU Schedule RL, "also includes distribution"; BGE's proposed delivery rate for Schedule R is flat across all hours, while Schedule RD has separate on-peak and off-peak delivery rates) [@velez_Docket9888Direct_2026].

[^smart]: [Karas Direct](https://pub.switch.box/karas_Docket9888Direct_2026) at 20:5–8 [@karas_Docket9888Direct_2026].

## VIII. Conclusion

**Q.** Does this conclude your surrebuttal testimony?

**A.** Yes, it does.
